title: "If he said it, it is true"
hook: Mecca mocks the night journey, and Abu Bakr says, if he said it, it is true (sirah)
carry: he weighed the speaker, not the distance

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musa, and fifty become five. Your line was: five, weighing fifty.

Morning in Mecca. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people what happened in the night: he was carried to Jerusalem and brought back before dawn. In the sirah the reaction is fast. Some laugh. Ibn Ishaq reports that some who had believed turned back. A caravan takes a month to get there and a month to return, people say, and he did it in one night? A few of them hurry off to find his close friend, Abu Bakr. Have you heard what your companion is saying now? Today: al-Siddiq.
screen: `CARRIED BY NIGHT.` → `MECCA LAUGHS.` → `THEY RUN TO ABU BAKR.`

segments.voice: Abu Bakr asks one question first: did he say that? Yes, they say. In Ibn Ishaq's account he answers: if he said it, then it is true. And he adds, roughly: why are you so surprised? He tells me news comes to him from heaven, from God, in an hour of the night or the day, and I believe him in that. This is further than Jerusalem. Then Abu Bakr goes to the Prophet and asks him to describe the city, and as he does, Abu Bakr keeps saying: you have spoken the truth. Tradition says this is the day he was called al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Bukhari has a report from the Prophet's side of that morning: when Quraysh would not believe him, Allah showed him Jerusalem, and he described it to them while looking at it. Notice what Abu Bakr's trust rests on. Not a feeling about miracles, but long knowledge of one man, and of what he has said before. He doesn't weigh the distance to Jerusalem. He weighs the speaker. And with his answer, this part of the story, sorrow, Ta'if and the night journey, comes to its close. It began with two graves, Khadijah's and Abu Talib's. It closes with a friend who stays when others mock.
screen: `DID HE SAY THAT?` · `IF HE SAID IT, IT IS TRUE.` · `HE WEIGHS THE SPEAKER.` · `AL-SIDDIQ: THE ONE WHO AFFIRMS.` · then, large: `IF HE SAID IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose word has held, again and again: someone who said they'd come, and came, who told you the hard thing when the easy thing was right there. Let their face settle in front of you, and notice how much of your life rests, quietly, on people like this. If you pray, you can thank God for that person by name.
Al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Abu Bakr's title, earned when he trusted the Prophet's word about the night journey without arguing the distance. Today's word.
Your line: he weighed the speaker, not the distance. Trust like that is built long before it's needed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Bakr by the title al-Siddiq and retell his answer when they recall the night journey, often on the night of al-Isra wal-Mi'raj.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abu Bakr believed something hard to believe.
what it means: he didn't weigh the distance to Jerusalem; he weighed the man who said it.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account of the morning after the isra; Bukhari's report that Jerusalem was shown to the Prophet as he described it; tradition ties the title al-Siddiq to this day.

chat.says: Why did Abu Bakr believe the night journey story so quickly?
options: He knew the Prophet's word; he weighed the speaker, not the distance.
He agreed so the crowd would stop laughing at his friend.
Because most people in Mecca already believed the story by then.
chat.meaning: He asked only: did he say that? Then: if he said it, it is true. His trust rested on long knowledge of the man.

al-Siddiq.meaning: the one who affirms the truth; Abu Bakr's title

Quraysh.meaning: the tribe that led Mecca, the Prophet's own

Bukhari.meaning: compiler of a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

notes: Abu Bakr's words and the crowd's caravan objection (a month there, a month back) are paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm.
'Tradition says this is the day he was called al-Siddiq': the link between the title and this event is reported in the sirah and some hadith collections; confirm the framing.
Bukhari 3886 cited for Jerusalem being shown to him; confirm the number.
